# Psalm 114 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Psalm

Psalm 114 is the second of the "Egyptian Hallel" psalms (Psalms 113–118), sung at the Passover meal. It celebrates the Exodus as the birth of Israel as God's covenant people. Spurgeon calls it "this sublime SONG OF THE EXODUS" and says, "True poetry has here reached its climax: no human mind has ever been able to equal, much less to excel, the grandeur of this Psalm."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps114.php

Ellicott notes the psalm's artistic mastery: the Divine name is withheld until v. 7, heightening the dramatic effect.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/114.htm

The Pulpit Commentary treats it as a psalm of reminiscence designed to encourage exiles returning from Babylon: "If God had done so much for them when he brought them out of Egypt … might they not be sure that his hand would be stretched out for them now?"
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-114.html

---

## v. 1 — "When Israel departed from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of foreign tongue"

**Traditional reading:** The verse opens the psalm with a burst of poetic energy. Israel's deliverance from Egypt is the central Old Covenant act of redemption, constantly to be remembered (Guzik). Spurgeon says the song "begins with a burst, as if the poetic fury could not be restrained, but overleaped all bounds."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps114.php

**"People of foreign tongue"** — This emphasizes Israel's alienation in Egypt. Guzik notes that though they lived there over 400 years, "it was never their home." Gill remarks that the Egyptian language was "barbarous" to Hebrew ears; the word carries a sense of oppression (cf. Isaiah 28:11; Jeremiah 5:15).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm

**Ellicott** adds that the Hebrew word, like the Greek *barbaros*, "implies a certain scorn or ridicule, which ancient races generally had for those speaking another language."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/114.htm

**Typological readings:** Gill sees this as an emblem of effectual calling — coming "out of bondage into liberty, out of darkness into light." The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary similarly treats the psalm as "typical of man's deliverance from sin's bondage, oppression, depression, and condemnation today."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-114.html

---

## v. 2 — "Judah became God's sanctuary, and Israel His dominion."

**Traditional reading:** The whole people became God's dwelling place and His kingdom. Guzik notes: "The leading tribe of Israel (Judah) represented the whole nation which became the dwelling place of God (His sanctuary)." Also: "Any place God dwells, He dominates."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**Spurgeon** observes the literary artistry: the pronoun "his" appears twice without naming God — the poet "is so full of thought concerning the Lord that he forgets to mention his name." This withholding of the Divine name builds suspense until v. 7. The whole people were "the shrine of Deity, and their camp was one great temple."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps114.php

**Gill** emphasizes that this is not merely the tribe of Judah but all the tribes; nevertheless a Jewish tradition (Jarchi, Kimchi) holds that Judah's tribe went into the Red Sea first, the others following. Spiritually, Gill sees this as typical of believers who are "the Lord's sanctuary, in which he dwells."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm

**Ellicott** notes that the feminine verb form ("became") shows the *land* is intended, not just the tribe: "the parallelism directs us to think … of the whole country."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/114.htm

**Calvin** (as excerpted in search results) writes: "In delivering his people, God erected a kingdom for himself and procured respect for his sacred name." He argues against limiting the reference to the tribe of Judah alone — the honor ascribed to Judah "belongs equally to the whole body of the people."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-114.html

**Matthew Henry** summarizes: "Judah was his sanctuary … Israel his dominion" means God set up his tabernacle among them and they came under his special protection.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/psalms-114.html

---

## v. 3 — "The sea observed and fled; the Jordan turned back"

**Traditional reading:** The Red Sea and the Jordan River — the beginning and end of Israel's wilderness journey — are paired as parallel miracles. Guzik cites Morgan: "It is noticeable that the Exodus is thought of in its completeness; not only escape from Egypt, but entrance to the land."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**The Pulpit Commentary** states: "These two marvels marked respectively the beginning and the end of Israel's long journey" (Cheyne).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-114.html

**Spurgeon** draws spiritual significance: "The division of the sea and the drying up of the river are placed together though forty years intervened, because they were the opening and closing scenes of one great event. We may thus unite by faith our new birth and our departure out of the world into the promised inheritance … the beginning ensures the end."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**Gill** notes the Targum's reading: "When the Word of the Lord appeared at it" — the sea *saw* the divine presence. He adds a typological layer: "Jordan was driven back … was an emblem of death, through which the saints pass to glory, which is abolished by Christ."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm

**Ellicott** makes the point that the Hebrew verb for Jordan's "turning back" does not suggest a parting asunder but a *turning backwards* of the descending stream — citing Stanley's *Jewish Church*.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/114.htm

---

## v. 4 — "The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs"

**Traditional reading:** This refers to the earthquake at Mount Sinai when God gave the Law (Exodus 19:16-20). The mountains shook and "skipped" like frightened — or joyful — sheep.

**Guzik** notes that the Hebrew word for "skipped" also carries the thought of joy: "creation was happy God brought this deliverance to His people." He quotes VanGemeren: "nature … responded with a twofold response: fear and great joy."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**Spurgeon** says: "Men fear the mountains, but the mountains tremble before the Lord." He adds a spiritual application: "Even thus do mountains of sin and hills of trouble move when the Lord comes forth to lead his people to their eternal Canaan."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps114.php

**Ellicott** notes that the Hebrew word is translated "dance" in Ecclesiastes 3:4 and that "the leaping of the hills formed part of every theophany."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/114.htm

**Gill** adds a typological reading: these mountains and hills "may represent the greater and lesser governors in the Roman empire … which skipped, and trembled … at the downfall of Paganism and progress of Christianity" (citing Revelation 6:14).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm

**The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** sees mountains and hills as "symbols of world powers, trembling before God, as Sinai did."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-114.html

---

## vv. 5-6 — "Why was it, O sea, that you fled … O mountains, that you skipped like rams?"

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist uses the poetic device of apostrophe — directly questioning inanimate nature — to dramatize the wonder of God's power. The questions are rhetorical and build toward the revelation of God in v. 7.

**Guzik** says the psalmist "challenged both the sea and the mountains. They were powerless to stand against the mighty presence of God. It's even more foolish to think that mankind … can stand against God's mighty presence."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**Spurgeon** applies this to human insensibility: "A gracious mind will chide human nature for its strange insensibility, when the sea and the river, the mountains and the hills, are all sensitive to the presence of God. … God has come nearer to us than ever he did to Sinai, or to Jordan, for he has assumed our nature, and yet the mass of mankind are neither driven back from their sins, nor moved in the paths of obedience."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps114.php

**The Pulpit Commentary** describes this as the psalmist "apostrophizing the sea, the Jordan, the mountains, and the lesser hills, inquiring of them for what reason they had forsaken their nature and done such strange things."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-114.html

---

## v. 7 — "Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob"

**Traditional reading:** This is the dramatic climax. Only here does the psalmist finally name the One whose presence caused all this upheaval: *Adonai* (the Lord, the Master) and *the God of Jacob*. The answer to the questions of vv. 5-6 is implicit: it was the presence of God Himself.

**Guzik** (quoting Boice): "The author must have been having fun as he wrote, knowing the answer … but holding it off. … For twelve lines he has allowed our interest to build for dramatic effect."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**Ellicott** calls the introduction of the answer "consummate art" and notes the Hebrew verb for "tremble" literally means "be in travail" — suggesting birth pangs. Morgan linked this to the birth of the nation.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/114.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**The Expositor's Bible Commentary** says: "Now the psalmist can peal forth the Name of Him, the sight of whom wrought these wonders. … He is still Lord of Nature. And, more blessed still, the Lord of Nature is the God of Jacob."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-114.html

**Calvin** understands this as an imperative ("Tremble!") — the prophet again appeals to the earth so that human hearts may be "more sensibly moved." He notes that the title *Adonai* signifies a "Lord or a Master," and the name "God of Jacob" is used "for the purpose of banishing from men all notions of false gods."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-114.html

**Gill** notes that some versions (Syriac, Arabic, Septuagint, Vulgate) render this in the past tense: "the earth *is moved* at the presence of the Lord." He explains it as a *prosopopoeia*: "Is it to be wondered at, that we, the sea, the river … have fled … when the whole earth … has trembled at the presence of God?"
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm

## v. 8 — "Who turned the rock into a pool, the flint into a fountain of water!"

**Traditional reading:** The psalm closes by recalling another Exodus miracle: God bringing water from the rock at Rephidim (Exodus 17:6) and Kadesh (Numbers 20:11). This demonstrates that God's power is not only for spectacular cosmic signs but also for tender, practical provision.

**Guzik:** "As Psalm 113 closed with God's compassion on the barren woman, this psalm closes with God's compassion on thirsty Israel. His great power and might are not merely for the dividing of waters and the shaking of mountains. His majestic might brings blessing to His people one by one."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**Spurgeon** applies it spiritually: "He supplies our temporal needs from sources of the most unlikely kind … As for our spiritual necessities they are all met by the water and the blood which gushed of old from the riven rock, Christ Jesus."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps114.php

**Gill** also typologically identifies the rock as Christ: "This was a type of Christ the Rock; who has an abiding fulness of grace in him; is the fountain of it, from whence it flows in great abundance for the supply of his people's wants."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm

**Matthew Henry** makes the same Christological connection: "That rock was Christ. The Son of God, the Rock of ages, gave himself to death, to open a fountain to wash away sins, and to supply believers with waters of life and consolation."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/114.htm

**Meyer** (quoted by Guzik) applies it devotionally: "This is a miracle which we all need to have wrought in our experience. Our heart is flint, our eyes are dry, our souls fail to respond with tears and regrets to the love of the Pierced One."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

**The Expositor's Bible Commentary** notes the psalm's abrupt ending: the singer "drops his harp without a formal close. The effect is all the greater." Maclaren says: "He has no word of 'moral,' no application, counsel, warning, or encouragement to give. Whoso will can draw these. Enough for him to lift his soaring song, and to check it into silence in the midst of its full music."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-114.html

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**No major doctrinal disagreements** emerge among Protestant traditions on this psalm, since it is a historical-reminiscence psalm narrating the Exodus. However, differences of *emphasis* can be observed:

- **Reformed (Calvin):** Emphasizes God's sovereignty in "erecting a kingdom for himself" through the deliverance and stresses the use of the name *Adonai* (Lord/Master) to assert divine rule over all earth. Calvin sees the imperatival "Tremble!" as a call to human hearts to be moved.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-114.html

- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill, Garner-Howes):** Strong emphasis on typology — the Exodus as a picture of individual conversion and the Christian life. Gill explicitly reads the sea, Jordan, mountains, and rock all as types of spiritual realities. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary applies the psalm forward to the Second Advent, where "heathen, Gentile world dominions fall before the Lord."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps114.php
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/114.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-114.html

- **Charismatic/Evangelical (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Emphasizes the *personal* application — noting that Jesus sang this psalm the night He was betrayed (Matthew 26:30), connecting the Exodus to Christ's greater deliverance. Guzik also stresses the emotional responses of nature (fear *and* joy) and the "dramatic effect" of the literary structure.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-114/

- **Anglican (Ellicott, Cambridge Bible):** Ellicott focuses on literary artistry — the psalm's structure, the suspense in withholding God's name, the use of apostrophe. The Cambridge Bible notes the psalm was used in Western liturgy from the sixth century "in the last offices for the dying and at the burial of the dead," and as a Proper Psalm for Easter Day. It also notes Dante's use of Psalm 114 (*In exitu Israel de Aegypto*) as the song of spirits entering Purgatory.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/114.htm
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/114.htm

## Other Views

**Liturgical use:** The Cambridge Bible notes that Psalm 114, as part of the Hallel, became a Proper Psalm for Easter Day in Western churches and was used at burials and the last offices for the dying, interpreting it mystically of "the exodus of the soul from the bondage of the flesh into the rest of God." Dante placed it in the mouths of spirits crossing to Purgatory (*Purgatorio* 2.46).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/114.htm

**Modern scholarship / other views:** My searches for netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com), and Pentecostal-specific (samstorms.org, ag.org) sources were cut off by tool limits. No results from those sites could be fetched.

---

*Summary:* Psalm 114 is a tightly crafted Passover song recalling the Exodus as Israel's birth as God's people. All surveyed commentators agree on its historical referents (Red Sea, Jordan, Sinai, water from the rock) and its literary brilliance — especially the delayed revelation of God's name until v. 7. Differences among traditions are in *application*: Reformed teachers emphasize divine sovereignty; Baptist and Evangelical teachers stress personal conversion typology and Christ as the Rock; Anglican scholars highlight the psalm's liturgical and literary artistry. Across all traditions, the psalm is read Christologically, noting that Jesus Himself sang it at the Last Supper.
